title: Seen the present, seen all
hookLine: whoever has seen the present has seen everything (Meditations 6.37)

cards: A complaint that a relative hasn't written. A request for money. Greetings to everyone at home.
Those lines could come from this week's texts, and some readers find the same lines in letters that survive from the ancient world. Lovers' names scratched on a wall. Jokes.
Insults. The costumes change; the scenes don't seem to. In book six, Marcus Aurelius draws a startling conclusion about time from exactly that sameness.

teach.b: Meditations six, thirty-seven, in George Long's translation: "He who has seen present things has seen all."
Everything that has happened from eternity, Marcus goes on, and everything that will happen without end, because all things are of one kin and one form.
Weddings, funerals, lawsuits, feasts, people flattering and people grieving: Marcus seems to think human life runs on a small set of scenes, staged again and again with new actors.
Look closely at the present, and you've seen the pattern of every age.
Behind this, ancient writers report, the early Stoics taught that the whole universe moves in great cycles, so history repeats in its shape.
Not every reader today shares that picture of the cosmos, and Marcus himself sometimes holds it loosely. You don't need the cosmology to feel the point. The line can be heard two ways.
One is weary: nothing's new, so why bother.
The other is the way Marcus seems to mean it: the present is enough. You don't have to see the future to understand your life, or need the past to have been grander.
On his reading, what there is to learn about being human is happening right in front of you, at this kitchen table, on this bus.
And the week behind: back quickly, stepmother and mother, in and out, gymnasium, show me I'm wrong, letter by letter. Each was a way of seeing the present clearly.

how: Readers of Marcus sometimes use this line to steady themselves in the present, treating the ordinary scene in front of them as a full picture of human life rather than waiting for something new.

o: the emperor who said seeing the present is seeing every age
a prophet who claimed to foresee the empire's future
a historian who wrote the story of Rome's past

games.q: seen the present, seen all — tap the pairs.
p: of one kin and one form

s: Marcus says the present shows you everything past and future
because, he says, all things are of one kin and one form.
this line only works if the Stoic cosmic cycles are true
the point that the present is enough stands without the cosmology.

games.q: you feel your ordinary life is too small to teach you anything. what does Marcus's line suggest?
o: look closely at the present; the whole pattern is there.
games.why: Meditations 6.37: he who has seen present things has seen all.

practice: Let your eyes rest on whatever is in front of you, and look at it as if it were the only scene there has ever been: the light, the sounds, someone moving in the next room.
People in Marcus's day sat in light like this, heard sounds like these, and waited for someone they loved to come home. Stay with this moment, looking.

wordCard.voice: Marcus, who claimed that a close look at the present shows the pattern of every age. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: seen it all. The present, looked at closely, is enough. Day five hundred eighty-one, and a week complete.
